title: Present Simple
theory:
## When do we use it?
Use the Present Simple to talk about habits, facts, schedules, and general truths — things that are always or usually true.

## How to form
With I / You / We / They → use the base verb.
With He / She / It → add -s (or -es / -ies).

### Spelling of the -s form
• Most verbs: add -s → work / works, eat / eats
• After -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: add -es → watch / watches, go / goes
• Consonant + y: change to -ies → study / studies, try / tries
• Irregular: have → has, do → does

## Negative & question
• Negative: I/You/We/They + don't + verb · He/She/It + doesn't + verb
• Question: Do / Does + subject + verb …?

## Examples
> I drink coffee every morning.
> She lives in Hanoi.
> The sun rises in the east.
> Do you play football? — Yes, I do.
> He doesn't eat meat.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ She go to school → ✅ She goes to school.
• ❌ He don't like rain → ✅ He doesn't like rain.
• ❌ I am play tennis → ✅ I play tennis.

title: Articles: a / an / the
theory:
## What is an article?
Articles are small words (a / an / the) used before a noun to say whether it is general or specific, known or unknown.

## a vs an
• Use a before a consonant SOUND: a book, a car, a university (sounds like "yu")
• Use an before a vowel SOUND: an apple, an hour (silent h), an honest answer

## the
Use the when both speaker and listener know exactly which thing is meant.
• Specific or already mentioned: I saw a dog. The dog was big.
• One-of-a-kind: the sun, the moon, the sky, the world
• Superlatives: the best, the largest
• Musical instruments: She plays the piano.

## No article
Use no article for general or uncountable nouns and for most names of people, cities, languages, meals.
• I love music. (in general)
• He speaks Vietnamese.
• We had dinner at 8.

## Examples
> I want an apple, please.
> She is a teacher.
> The book on the table is mine.
> Honesty is the best policy.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ She is teacher → ✅ She is a teacher.
• ❌ I love the music → ✅ I love music. (in general)
• ❌ An university → ✅ A university (sound starts with "yu").

title: Prepositions: in / on / at
theory:
## Quick rule of thumb
Think of size: at = a single point · on = a surface or line · in = inside something.

## For TIME
### at — clock times & specific moments
• at 7 PM, at noon, at midnight, at sunset
• at night, at the weekend (UK), at Christmas

### on — days & dates
• on Monday, on Friday morning
• on April 5, on my birthday

### in — months, years, seasons, parts of the day
• in January, in 2025, in summer
• in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening
• in a few minutes (future)

## For PLACE
### at — specific point or address
• at the door, at the bus stop, at home
• at school (= attending it), at work

### on — surfaces and lines
• on the table, on the wall, on the floor
• on the second floor, on the corner

### in — enclosed spaces / large areas
• in the box, in the room, in the car
• in Hanoi, in Vietnam, in the world

## Examples
> I'll see you on Monday at 9 AM.
> She was born in May 1998.
> The cat is in the box, on the chair, at the corner.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ In Monday → ✅ On Monday.
• ❌ At the morning → ✅ In the morning.
• ❌ On Hanoi → ✅ In Hanoi (cities use 'in').

title: Present Continuous
theory:
## When do we use it?
Use the Present Continuous (am / is / are + V-ing) for actions happening RIGHT NOW or AROUND now, temporary situations, and planned future arrangements.

## How to form
Subject + am / is / are + verb-ing
• I am
• You / We / They are
• He / She / It is

### Spelling of -ing
• Most verbs: add -ing → work / working
• Ending in -e (silent): drop -e → make / making
• Short verb + consonant: double the consonant → run / running, sit / sitting
• Ending in -ie: change to -y + ing → lie / lying

## Negative & question
• Negative: subject + am/is/are + not + V-ing
• Question: Am / Is / Are + subject + V-ing …?

## Time markers
now, right now, at the moment, today, this week, currently, Look!, Listen!

## Examples
> I am studying English now.
> Look! It's raining.
> She is working in Singapore this month.
> Are you watching TV? — No, I'm not.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ I working now → ✅ I am working now.
• ❌ He is run → ✅ He is running.
• ❌ She is knowing the answer → ✅ She knows the answer. (state verbs don't take -ing)

title: Past Simple
theory:
## When do we use it?
Use the Past Simple for finished actions in the past — with a clear past time or simply understood as completed.

## How to form
### Regular verbs: add -ed
• work → worked, play → played, watch → watched
• Ending in -e: just add -d → live → lived
• Consonant + y: change to -ied → study → studied, try → tried
• Short verb + consonant: double consonant + ed → stop → stopped

### Irregular verbs (memorize)
• go → went, eat → ate, see → saw, have → had, do → did, take → took, give → gave, come → came, get → got, make → made, say → said, find → found, buy → bought, think → thought

## Be: was / were
• I / He / She / It → was
• You / We / They → were

## Negative & question
• Negative: subject + did not (didn't) + base verb
• Question: Did + subject + base verb …?
• With be: was/were + not, Was/Were + subject …?

## Time markers
yesterday, last week / month / year, two days ago, in 2010, when I was a child

## Examples
> I went to Hanoi last summer.
> She didn't eat breakfast yesterday.
> Did you call him? — Yes, I did.
> They were at school on Monday.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ I didn't went → ✅ I didn't go. (after did/didn't use base form)
• ❌ Did you saw him? → ✅ Did you see him?
• ❌ He goed home → ✅ He went home.

title: Past Continuous
theory:
## When do we use it?
Use the Past Continuous (was / were + V-ing) for:
• An action in progress at a specific moment in the past.
• A background action interrupted by a shorter Past Simple action.
• Two parallel actions happening at the same time.

## How to form
Subject + was / were + verb-ing
• I / He / She / It → was + V-ing
• You / We / They → were + V-ing

## Negative & question
• Negative: was / were + not + V-ing
• Question: Was / Were + subject + V-ing …?

## With Past Simple (key pattern)
Use **while / as** + Past Continuous for the longer background action; **when** + Past Simple for the shorter event.
• While I was reading, the phone rang.
• When she arrived, we were having dinner.

## Time markers
at 8 PM yesterday, all morning, while, when, as, this time last week

## Examples
> I was sleeping at midnight.
> They were playing tennis at 5 PM.
> What were you doing when I called?
> The sun was shining and the birds were singing.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ I was play → ✅ I was playing.
• ❌ When she called, I cooked → ✅ When she called, I was cooking. (background)
• ❌ We was working → ✅ We were working.

title: Present Perfect
description: I have worked here for 5 years
theory:
## When do we use it?
Use the Present Perfect (have / has + past participle) to CONNECT the past with NOW. Three main uses:
1. Life experience (no specific time) — *I have visited Paris.*
2. Recently completed action with present result — *She has lost her keys.*
3. Unfinished action that started in the past and continues — *We have lived here for 10 years.*

## How to form
Subject + have / has + past participle (V3)
• I / You / We / They → have
• He / She / It → has

### Past participle (V3) examples
• Regular: worked, played, lived (= same as V2)
• Irregular: gone, eaten, seen, had, done, taken, given, come, got/gotten, made, said, found, bought, thought, written, drunk

## Negative & question
• Negative: have/has + not (haven't / hasn't) + V3
• Question: Have/Has + subject + V3 …?

## Key words
ever, never, already, yet, just, for + duration, since + point in time

## Examples
> I have already finished my homework.
> She has just arrived.
> Have you ever been to Japan? — No, I haven't.
> We've known each other for ten years.
> He hasn't called me since Monday.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ I have went → ✅ I have gone.
• ❌ I have seen him yesterday → ✅ I saw him yesterday. (specific past time → Past Simple)
• ❌ She lives here for 5 years → ✅ She has lived here for 5 years.

title: Future with will
theory:
## When do we use it?
Use "will" + base verb for:
• Predictions and beliefs about the future — *It will rain tomorrow.*
• Decisions made at the moment of speaking — *I'll have the chicken, please.*
• Promises, offers, and willingness — *I'll help you.*
• Future facts — *I will be 30 next year.*

## How to form
Subject + will + base verb (same for all subjects)
• Contracted: I'll, you'll, he'll, she'll, we'll, they'll
• Negative: will not = won't
• Question: Will + subject + base verb …?

## Time markers
tomorrow, next week / month / year, in 2030, soon, in a few minutes, one day, probably

## With "I think / I'm sure / probably"
> I think it will be sunny tomorrow.
> She probably won't come.

## Examples
> I'll call you later.
> They will arrive at 8 PM.
> Don't worry, I won't tell anyone.
> Will you marry me?

## Common mistakes
• ❌ I will to call you → ✅ I will call you. (no "to")
• ❌ He will calls → ✅ He will call. (base form, no -s)
• ❌ Will you to help me? → ✅ Will you help me?

title: Future with be going to
description: I am going to work tomorrow
theory:
## When do we use it?
Use "be going to" + base verb for:
• Plans and intentions decided BEFORE now — *I'm going to study tonight.*
• Predictions based on present evidence — *Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.*

## How to form
Subject + am / is / are + going to + base verb
• I am going to
• You / We / They are going to
• He / She / It is going to

## Negative & question
• Negative: am / is / are + not + going to
• Question: Am / Is / Are + subject + going to …?

## will vs. be going to (quick guide)
• Spontaneous decision (right now) → *will*
> The phone is ringing. I'll get it!
• Plan made earlier → *be going to*
> I'm going to visit my parents this weekend. (planned days ago)
• Prediction with no evidence → *will*
> I think Vietnam will win.
• Prediction with evidence in front of you → *be going to*
> She has no umbrella — she's going to get wet!

## Examples
> We're going to buy a new car.
> Are you going to study tonight?
> He isn't going to come to the meeting.
> Look! The vase is going to fall!

## Common mistakes
• ❌ I going to go → ✅ I am going to go.
• ❌ She is going to be travel → ✅ She is going to travel.
• ❌ Are you go to study? → ✅ Are you going to study?

title: Comparatives & Superlatives
theory:
## When do we use them?
• **Comparative** — compare TWO things: *Mai is taller than Linh.*
• **Superlative** — compare ONE thing with all others: *Mai is the tallest in the class.*

## How to form
### Short adjectives (1 syllable)
• Add -er / -est: tall → taller → the tallest
• Ending in -e: just add -r / -st: nice → nicer → nicest
• Consonant + y: change to -ier / -iest: happy → happier → the happiest
• Short vowel + consonant: double consonant: big → bigger → the biggest

### Long adjectives (2+ syllables)
• Use more / the most: beautiful → more beautiful → the most beautiful
• important → more important → the most important

### Two syllables ending in -y → -ier / -iest
busy → busier → busiest, easy → easier → easiest

### Irregular
good → better → the best
bad → worse → the worst
far → farther / further → the farthest / furthest
little → less → the least
much / many → more → the most

## Patterns
• A is ___-er than B / A is more ___ than B
• A is the ___-est (of / in …) / A is the most ___ (of / in …)
• Use "in" with places: the tallest IN the class
• Use "of" with groups / time: the best OF all, the hottest OF the year

## Examples
> Tokyo is bigger than Hanoi.
> This is the most expensive phone in the shop.
> She runs faster than I do.
> Today is the hottest day of the year.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ more big → ✅ bigger
• ❌ the most happiest → ✅ the happiest
• ❌ taller that → ✅ taller than
• ❌ He is gooder → ✅ He is better.

title: Modal verbs
theory:
## What are modal verbs?
Modal verbs are helper verbs (can, could, should, must, may, might, would) that add meaning like ability, permission, advice, obligation, or possibility.

## How to use
Subject + modal + base verb (no "to", no -s, no -ing)
• I can swim.
• She must go.
• He should rest.

### Negative & question
• Negative: modal + not (can't, shouldn't, mustn't, may not)
• Question: modal + subject + base verb …?

## Main modals & meanings
### can / could
• Ability — *I can speak English. She could swim at 5.*
• Permission (informal) — *Can I come in?*
• Possibility — *It can be cold here in winter.*

### should
• Advice — *You should see a doctor.*
• Mild obligation — *We should be quiet in the library.*

### must / have to
• Strong obligation / rule — *You must wear a helmet.*
• Logical certainty — *You haven't eaten. You must be hungry.*
• mustn't = forbidden; don't have to = not necessary

### may / might
• Possibility (uncertain) — *It may rain. He might come.*
• may = polite permission — *May I leave early?*

### would
• Polite request — *Would you help me?*
• Hypothetical — *I would travel more if I had money.*

## Examples
> I can play the guitar.
> You shouldn't smoke.
> Students must arrive on time.
> Could you open the window, please?

## Common mistakes
• ❌ He cans swim → ✅ He can swim. (no -s)
• ❌ I must to go → ✅ I must go. (no "to")
• ❌ She should goes → ✅ She should go.

title: Question words (Wh-)
theory:
## The Wh- family
The main question words are: **what, where, when, who, whose, which, why, how**.

## What each one asks about
• **What** — thing, action, idea: *What is your name?*
• **Where** — place: *Where do you live?*
• **When** — time: *When is your birthday?*
• **Who** — person (subject / object): *Who is that?*
• **Whose** — possession: *Whose car is this?*
• **Which** — choice from a limited set: *Which color do you prefer, red or blue?*
• **Why** — reason: *Why are you sad?*
• **How** — manner, condition: *How are you?*

## "How" combinations
• **How much** — uncountable amount / price: *How much milk? How much is it?*
• **How many** — countable quantity: *How many books?*
• **How long** — duration: *How long does it take?*
• **How often** — frequency: *How often do you exercise?*
• **How old** — age: *How old are you?*
• **How far** — distance: *How far is the station?*

## Question structure
• With "be": Wh- + be + subject (+ …)? → *Where are you?*
• With other verbs: Wh- + do / does / did + subject + base verb? → *What do you eat?*
• When Wh- is the subject, no auxiliary: *Who lives here? What happened?*

## Examples
> Where is the bathroom?
> When did you arrive?
> How many siblings do you have?
> Why didn't you call me?
> Whose phone is ringing?

## Common mistakes
• ❌ Where you live? → ✅ Where do you live?
• ❌ How much books? → ✅ How many books? (countable)
• ❌ Who do live here? → ✅ Who lives here? (Who = subject)

title: Countable vs Uncountable
theory:
## What's the difference?
• **Countable** nouns can be counted: 1 book, 2 books · 1 apple, 5 apples. They have singular AND plural forms.
• **Uncountable** nouns CANNOT be counted as individual items: water, music, advice, money, information. They have NO plural form and take a singular verb.

## Common uncountable nouns
food / drink: water, milk, bread, rice, sugar, cheese
abstract: information, advice, news, music, work, help, time, money
substances: air, sand, gold, paper, hair (when general)

> ⚠️ "News", "advice", "information", "furniture", "luggage" are uncountable in English even though they may be countable in Vietnamese.

## a / an, some, any
• **a / an** — only with singular countable: *a book, an apple* (NOT *a water*)
• **some** — positive sentences (both): *I have some books. I want some water.*
• **any** — negatives & questions (both): *I don't have any money. Do you have any sisters?*

## much / many / a lot of
• **much** — uncountable: *How much water? Not much time.*
• **many** — plural countable: *How many friends? Too many cars.*
• **a lot of** / **lots of** — both: *a lot of water, a lot of friends*

## few / little
• **a few** — small but enough (countable): *I have a few questions.*
• **a little** — small but enough (uncountable): *I have a little money.*

## Counting uncountables
Use a "unit" word: a glass of water, a piece of advice, a slice of bread, two cups of coffee, a bottle of milk.

## Examples
> Can I have some water, please?
> How many eggs do we need?
> She doesn't have much free time.
> I'd like a piece of cake.

## Common mistakes
• ❌ How much books? → ✅ How many books?
• ❌ I need an advice → ✅ I need some advice / a piece of advice.
• ❌ Many money → ✅ Much money / a lot of money.
• ❌ He has many homeworks → ✅ He has a lot of homework. (uncountable, no plural)
